en: The Five Stages.
[1] The First Stage: Vajra Recitation. Oṃ, homage to the Buddha.
Having bowed to the Protector who is the essence of all Buddhas, the glorious Mahāsukha,
I shall explain the sequence of Vajra-recitation in accordance with the Yoga Tantras.
For those established in the stage of generation who desire the stage of completion,
this method has been fashioned by the Perfect Buddhas like a staircase.
The one called wind is the life-force of sentient beings, the performer of all actions;
it is the vehicle of consciousness, fivefold in nature and further divided tenfold.
Following the sequence of the wind-element, one should enter the reality of mantra;
having attained mastery over mantra, one becomes well-trained in vajra-recitation.
The mantra practitioner, established in vajra-recitation, shall attain the profound realization of the mind;
abiding in the illusion-like samādhi, he shall enter into the limit of reality.
Arising from the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), one attains non-dual gnosis;
established in the samādhi of simultaneous union (yuganaddha), one is thereafter incapable of anything further.
This is called the yoga of completion, and he is Mahāvajradhara;
endowed with the excellence of all aspects, he then becomes omniscient.
The future, the past, and the present— the three times—
should be seen in their entirety in that very instant through the purity of luminosity.
This reality, established in the *Śrīsamāja* Tantra and well-sealed,
is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru according to the explanatory tantras.

In this regard, first of all, the introductory statement concerning the wind-element (*vāyutattva*) is introduced from the root sūtra itself: "One should contemplate a mustard seed at the tip of the nose; within that mustard seed, one should meditate upon the delightful locus of gnosis (*jñānapada*), the secret fashioned by gnosis, which contains all that is moving and stationary. (Pk 1.10)
One should always meditate with effort through yoga upon a great five-colored jewel, the size of a mustard seed, at the tip of the nose.
Thus, he provides the explanation of this vajra-word in the *Caturdevīvyākhyātantra* by means of intentional language (*sandhābhāṣā*):
"Therefore, O Goddess, I shall fully proclaim that which is more essential than the essence, the supreme secret of all Buddhas, which abides within the self of all. (Pk 1.12)
"The reality consisting of the five gnoses is the size of a mustard seed;
in its center resides the deity, who is unmanifest yet possesses a manifest form. (Pk 1.13)
The *Samājottara* also, illuminating this very point, says:
"One should expel the breath, which consists of the five gnoses and has the nature of the five elements, and imagine it in the form of a single mass at the tip of the lotus-nose. (Pk 1.14)
"The great jewel of five colors is known as *prāṇāyāma*.
Having meditated on one's own mantra in the heart, one should place the mind within the *bindu*.
Regarding this, the explanatory tantra named *Vajramālā* provides the following further instruction:
The visualization of the *prāṇāyāma* consists of a mustard seed at the tip of the nose;
from the state of Buddhahood, five rays of light abide within that *prāṇāyāma*.
Emerging above from the nose through the left, the right, both together, and being motionless—thus it is fourfold; for this reason, these are known as the internal times (velā).
One should indicate the coming and going [of the breath] at the lotuses of the throat, heart, navel, and secret place;
one should dwell for a period of half a watch (yāma) in regular succession according to the sequence.
The ray of light emerging from the south is that circle of fire;
this is clearly red in color, and Padmanātha is the deity here.
A ray of light emerging from the left is designated as the wind mandala;
it has the appearance of greenish-black, and Karmanātha is the deity here.
From these two, a ray of light emerges, yellow in color and of great brilliance;
this is the Maheśvara-maṇḍala, and Ratnanātha is the deity here.
Stable and of slow movement, resembling a white kunda flower or the moon, this is the mandala of Varuṇa; here, Vajranātha is the deity.
The wind that pervades the entire body and initiates all movements,
having the nature of Vairocana, shall emerge from the dead body.
This manifest wind-element has the nature of the five gnoses;
the logicians do not understand it, for it is inaccessible to immature yogins.
Having thus established the reality of wind, the introductory statement for the reality of mantra is now introduced from the Root Sūtra:

"The supreme secret, called the 'Exhortation of the Heart of All Tantras' and the 'Secret of the Body, Speech, and Mind of All Tathāgatas,' uttered the compendium of mantras through the verbal expression of the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind:
OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ."
Through the recitation that infers the meaning, which is without intrinsic nature and beautiful,
the investigation [arising] from the Buddhas of the three times is called Vajra-recitation.
One who subsists on alms should not perform recitation, nor should one be devoted to begging;
rather, one may enjoy all desired pleasures while reciting the mantra with undivided limbs.
This is the heading; its detailed explanation is set forth in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇavyākhyātantra*:
Then the glorious one replied to the pervasive Lord Mahāvairocana: "This mind is of universal form, according to the rebirths of all sentient beings. (Pk 1.27)

Although it is devoid of intrinsic nature once arisen, it is nevertheless designated as a "thing" because it arises dependently; and having correctly produced the experience of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), which is equal to space, [one should remain].
And in order to accomplish the welfare of the world, having understood that it is merely a means of accomplishment, it was explained in detail in the Tantra for the sake of superior persons.
"O Lord, those who come in the future will say, 'We are the teachers.
Having spoken thus, those fools cast aspersions on me, saying 'This is mine,' for they do not know the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) according to its true meaning. (Pk 1.30)
Just as the Blessed Lord, the all-pervading Mahāvairocana, spoke these words of praise three times to Vajrapāṇi: PK_1.31.
I shall explain in detail, according to the reality of non-conceptual meaning,
that which is called conventional and ultimate, consisting of verbal expression and perception.
For verbal expression is the commonality that apprehends the form of the Buddha;
it is the conventional reality known as the essence of mantra, while suchness is the ultimate reality.
One who is not bound by the ten [factors] from one up to nine should be known as unbound; he knows the supreme attainment.
He who knows the vowels and consonants, which follow the number nine,
as being unbound by mutual conjunction— he is the teacher of the world.
Joined with the end of the elements (bhūtānta), it abides in the sixteenth [digit] beginning with Kalā;
it is conjoined with five groups of five and arranged as four and three.
It should not have an anusvāra, nor be long, nor possess guṇa or saṃdhi, nor undergo elision;
it should be short, a complete sentence, neither multiple nor single.
Those phonemes which have been described as being behind, and those which are again facing forward—
these are female, male, and neuter, and they are conceptually constructed from the bases (dhātu) and so forth.
Having understood that which is joined above and below, one should apply it with the intellect;
this mantra, which is uttered, is born from the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature.
Then there is the transformed form which perceives the deity;
it is conventional, established in the three principles (tattvas), and characterized by the recitation and dissolution of primordial nature (prakṛti).
The knowledge that takes the syllable *A* as its object is the heart of the Buddha;
the syllable *Oṃ* emanates sentient beings fashioned in the supreme form of the Buddha.
The syllable *hūṃ* should withdraw sentient beings, and the syllable *āḥ* shall be the stabilizer;
likewise, there is entry, abiding, and emergence in due order.
Established in the state of wisdom and means, one should recite the mantra with its limbs unseparated;
the recitation of Pāṇḍarā and the others is prescribed as two hundred and twenty-five [times].
When correctly multiplied by four, the fourfold yoga is one hundred and nine;
that which is seen as nine hundred through twenty-four circumambulations becomes,
from the moment of its production, twelve thousand one hundred and sixty.
Illuminating this very point during the internal session, it is said in the *Samājottara*:

"By means of the ritual procedure of the Vidyā method, through the practice of the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*), one should recite the mantra whose limbs are indivisible, one hundred thousand times according to the count of syllables. (Pk 1.45)
The yogi should abandon external recitation, for it is an obstacle to meditative cultivation.
Since the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder whose very nature is the vajra, is the meaning of the mantra, how could he perform recitation here?
One obtains an elephant immediately by searching for the elephant's tracks;
since the mantra is itself the manifest form, what else could one seek? (1.47)
Moreover, O Vajradhṛk, a certain person endowed with the threefold union should perform the invocation, the dismissal, as well as the stabilization [of the deity]. (Pk 1.48)
Invocation is by means of entry; dismissal is by means of the swift [wind];
installation is by means of vapor; from that state of total confidence, supreme accomplishment arises.
When the disciple is in haste or weeping, the application of the mantra has been taught by the preceptor with great effort right at the base of the disciple's ear.
Now, having demonstrated the divine method of the masters of yoga,
I shall proclaim the secret syllable that bestows the fruit of yogic accomplishment.
By the mere thought of which, the yogins become bestowers of boons;
through the application of the first syllable, one always performs exhalation.
Endowed with the eight [vowels] and the letter *u* together with the bindu, the yogi emits the breath; this is here called "attainment through desire."
Twenty-two thousand, one thousand, and likewise six hundred;
this is the number of recitations the lord of yogins performs in a single day and night.
Thus, in this way, the subtle yoga has been revealed in the Guhyasandhi;
nevertheless, recitation (jāpa) is said to be free from meditation and study.
Having performed the service according to the ritual procedure by means of this vajra-recitation,
one should accomplish all activities through the illusion-like samādhi.
Regarding this, it is said in the *Advayasamatā-mahāyogatantra*:
"Having recited the incomparable mantra, the practitioner who is devoted to the means of accomplishment shall achieve success;
the three worlds will be accomplished for him in a single month—of this there is no doubt. (Pk 1.57)
Having recited six hundred thousand times the mantra born of primordial wisdom,
and having paid homage to Vajrasattva, he attains accomplishment on the full moon day.
No vow is prescribed for him, nor a rosary, nor a mantra;
the practices of meditative concentration and fire-offerings, as well as the higher and lower [paths], are all abandoned.
By means of the letter *ya*, whatever accomplishment one desires is brought about through the three [letters] beginning with *ra*. Thus proceeds the activity that is to be performed.
In the fire, wind, Indra, and Varuṇa mandalas,
two [deities] each remain engaged in their activity during the period of half a watch.
One who is devoted primarily to worship becomes worthy of worship; one who is devoted primarily to recitation is purified;
one intent on the fire-sacrifice attains prosperity; and one intent on meditation attains liberation.
Having understood this, the mantra-practitioner should then act like a child of the world;
thus, the mantras are accomplished through the single principle of non-conceptuality.
"This reality of mantra, which is the manifest accomplishment of the Vajra of Speech, should be applied to mind-only through the differentiation of the three types of gnosis. (Pk 1.64)

One who is deceitful and disrespectful toward the guru, one who is arrogant regarding mantras, one who is proud of his knowledge of books, one who lacks faith, or one who is devoid of initiation— the discourse concerning even the *krama* of such a person has not been spoken.
One who is faithful, devoted to the guru, and always intent on service—such a person should receive the oral instruction;
wealth is not to be considered. This grace of the guru is primarily dependent upon the guru himself.
Someone might leap from the summit of the king of mountains; though he does not desire to fall, he nevertheless falls.
Likewise, one who has received beneficial instruction through the grace of the Guru may not desire liberation, yet he is nonetheless liberated.
The Stage of Vajra Recitation is completed.
"This is the work of the venerable Nāgārjuna;
the extent of this treatise is seventy-six [verses]."
The first stage.
The second stage is the sequence of the purification of all purity, also known by the alternative name "Unsurpassed Junction.
Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva!
Homage be to you, homage be to you, homage be to you; homage again and again.
When praised in this way, homage be to you: who is the praiser, and who is the one praised?
Just as water poured into water, or ghee into ghee, one perceives one's own nature within oneself; where such knowledge exists here, that is true veneration.
However, that cannot be attained without resorting to the states of omniscience;
like an island shrouded by a veil of darkness, one may reach it through [the grace of] serenity.
The empty, the very empty, and the third, the great empty;
and the fourth, the all-empty, according to the distinction between fruit and cause.
From the union of wisdom and means, the "attainer" (upalabdhaka) is produced;
and from that produced attainer, the "all-empty" clear light arises.

But the state purified through the sequence of causes is attained by means of the union with the three consciousnesses and through the conjunction with the three voids; thus the unsurpassed state is reached.
Light, emptiness, wisdom, and the mind that is dependent—
now I shall clearly explain the manifestation of their primordial nature.
Dispassion is indeed moderate and likewise intense;
it is that which has entered and departed from the mind, and similarly, the third is grief and so forth.
Gentle trembling, fearful trembling, trembling with moderate fear, and trembling with extreme fear;
likewise, craving, moderate craving, excessive craving, and grasping.
The non-virtuous, as well as hunger and thirst, sensation and equal sensation,
intense sensation, the moment, the knower, the pierced, and the state of retention.
Discernment, shame, and compassion—these three arising from affection;
as well as trepidation, doubt, and envy—these are proclaimed [as the afflictions].
The thirty-three fundamental constituents of embodied beings, which are self-cognizable, are presented under the designation of "night" by way of their manifest conventional form. (Pk 2.12)
The female designation is likewise proclaimed, as well as the form of Mandā;
furthermore, there is the left-hand designation, which is the lotus within the lunar disc.
Because it serves as the cause for stabilization, the first vowel is accompanied by a bindu;
resembling the rays of the moon, it is the source of the knowledge of illumination.
That which is called "the appearance of light" is the method of the ultimate emptiness;
likewise, the imagined nature is so described, as is the mental factor.
Passion, the impassioned, as well as contentment, moderate contentment, and extreme contentment; exhilaration, joy, wonder, and likewise laughter. (Pk 2.16)
Delightful embracing, as well as kissing and sucking;
fortitude, virility, pride, and the powers of the agent and the appropriator.
Zeal and daring, as well as the highest daring,
middle daring, and the lowest daring, along with playfulness and even enmity.
Auspiciousness, eloquent speech, truth, falsehood, and likewise certainty;
non-attachment, generosity, incitement, and likewise heroism;
lack of shame, being rogue and wicked, as well as obstinacy and crookedness.
The forty fundamental natures are momentary, born from the utter void.
The perception of a man by day, and the right [hand] in the form of a donkey;
likewise, the perception of the solar disc and the perception of the vajra.
That very [energy] is to be known as Kalā, adorned with two points (bindus), resembling the rays of the sun, and born from the union of light and radiance. (Pk 2.22)
The perception of light, that which is perceived, the perfected nature, and ignorance—these are [the aspects] by name. // Pk_2.23 //
These are said by the Victors to be synonyms for the state of great emptiness:
the moment of intense passion, forgetfulness, and indeed delusion.
Silence, weariness, laziness, and likewise dullness—these seven moments of ignorance are to be recognized by subtle yogins. (2.25)
When the seed-syllable is not conjoined with the bindu, nor the breath has emerged through the gates,
that which is perceived as light is the characteristic of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa).
These sixty-one subtle constituent elements (prakṛtis) proceed during the day and likewise at night, driven by the force of the wind-vehicle.

In the *kṣaṇa*, the *lava*, the *muhūrta*, the *nimeṣa*, and likewise the *mātraka*: a *kṣaṇa* is the duration of a finger-snap; a *lava* is the time taken for a mustard seed to roll [off the tip of a finger]. (Pk 2.28)
A breath-hold (āśvāsa) lasts for a moment (muhūrta), while a nimeṣa is the closing of the eyes;
a mātrā is the clapping of hands—such is the definition of the kṣaṇa and other units of time.
Knowledge is mere consciousness, devoid of characteristics like space;
nevertheless, it possesses distinctions consisting of twilight, night, and day.
Light, the appearance of light, and likewise the attainment of light—the mind is said to be threefold; its basis is now described.
Knowledge, having become mixed with the subtle form of the wind,
issues forth through the pathways of the senses and takes hold of its objects.
When the wind, joined with the appearance [of light], has become the vehicle,
then it sets all its constituent elements into motion, both in their natural order and in their disordered state.
Wherever the wind is situated, it carries that very same nature;
as long as the arising of the breath continues, there will be no appearance of stillness.
The conceptualization of self-existence would be the cause for the two appearances;
it would consist of both parts when there is the perception of light.
Of all illusions, the illusion of a woman is preeminent;
this very distinction of the three types of knowledge is clearly perceived right here.
Passion, dispassion, and that which is between the two—this triad [arises] through the union of the two organs by means of the conjunction of the vajra and the lotus. (Pk 2.37)
The union of the two cognitions is proclaimed as "attainment" (samāpatti);
indeed, through the attainment of the two cognitions by means of performing what has been taught, [one attains it].
That knowledge which is attained through effort is the perceiver of light;
yet, for it, the union of the vajra and the lotus does not exist from the perspective of conventional reality.
Through the power of yoga, one who has experienced [this] even once attains accomplishment;
having understood the distinctions according to the natural functioning of knowledge.
The yogi should constantly observe that very same primordial nature (prakṛti), which, like clouds, appears in many forms with various shapes and colors. (Pk 2.41)
Just as [forms] arise from the expanse of the sky and indeed dissolve back into it,
so too do all natures have the three appearances as their cause.
Having experienced all sense objects, they enter the luminous state;
yet these beings remain veiled by the cataracts of ignorance regarding the knowledge of their own intrinsic nature.
Having performed wholesome or unwholesome karma, they wander through the five realms of existence;
having committed the immediate transgressions and the like, one ripens in the hells.
Having performed virtuous deeds such as giving, one is honored in the heavens and other realms;
and thus, after undergoing this again and again for thousands of endless births, [one eventually attains liberation].
Out of delusion, one grieves, thinking, "This is the ripening of past karma"—
that by which sentient beings are afflicted through the conjunction of the nature [of things] and appearances.
Having known that very [reality], the wise are liberated from the cage of existence;
this very nature of wisdom is like the conceptualization of the lunar disk.
One should see one's own mind itself as the lunar disc;
then, having focused upon that moon, one should visualize the vajra symbol.
For this indicates the skillful means for yogins who practice the generation of the vajra and so forth;
the union of the moon, vajra, and so on is the conjunction of mind and mental factors.
From the union of wisdom and means, the form of the deity arises;
having sealed oneself with the four mudrās, one should maintain the divine pride of the deity.
The mantra practitioner, possessing the yoga of the generation stage, should always move about,
as has been explained at great length in various places such as the *Śrī-guhyasamāja* and other tantras.
As long as there is the application of cultivation, one remains a beginner;
now, the indication of perfected yoga is being made.
The purification of the three voids is here called the Clear Light;
and that state of universal voidness arises from the purification of the three cognitions.
The reality that is the state of purified gnosis is unsurpassed omniscience;
it is changeless, without appearance, free from duality, and supremely auspicious.
It is neither "it exists" nor "it does not exist," for it is beyond the scope of verbal expression;
from this luminous and pure state, the threefold gnosis arises.
Bearing the thirty-two marks and endowed with the eighty minor characteristics,
possessed of the excellence of all aspects, he is then born as the omniscient one.
And so it is said in the Lalitavistara Mahāyāna Sūtra:
"This Śākyasiṃha, the Tathāgata, desires perfect awakening."
Out of the conceit that "I shall attain Buddhahood through great emptiness," he went to the bank of the Nairañjanā River and achieved the *āsphānaka* concentration.
Then the Victors, situated in the midst of space like sesame seeds filling [the vessel], spoke with a single voice to that son of the Victor: "Acchaṭa! (Pk 2.59)
This meditation is impure and does not bring about what is desired;
rather, one should take as an object that which is luminous, supreme, and like the expanse of space.
Having attained the state of luminosity, you arise in whatever form you desire;
likewise, having obtained all sovereign powers, you rejoice in the vajra-body.
Having heard that sound, the son of the Victor then released the *āsphānaka* [meditative absorption] and,
at the time of midnight, took hold of reality itself.
With body perfectly straight and speech likewise straightforward, he neither eats nor abstains from food; he is neither silent nor does he speak.
With eyes neither closed nor blinking, one perceives the pure, manifest, great gnosis—utterly empty and most wonderful. (Pk 2.64)
Then, through the grace of the Guru’s feet, he perceives that manifest reality—
the three worlds of the past, the future, and the present.
At that very moment, one who maintains the purity of luminosity should perceive everything as adorned with the qualities of illusion, such as the moon in water or a mirage.
At the time of sunrise, however, having sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree in the diamond-like samādhi, he performed the shattering of Māra.
Having attained the unsurpassed knowledge of reality, the Lord of the Śākyas has here demonstrated that very same [knowledge] for the sake of the welfare of the three worlds.
The realization of the truth is called the vision of perfect awakening;
even that man who has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution and possesses little merit, [attains it].
Through the grace of the Guru, one obtains another [state] like a wish-fulfilling gem;
he performs his conduct as he desires, being a fully awakened Buddha in the future.
Neither passion nor dispassion is found; the middle way is not apprehended.
Neither empty nor non-empty is the middle way apprehended.
This very *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga* has been revealed;
that reality which is distinct from the three cognitions was spoken with intentional terminology (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).
In the chapter on Bodhicitta, by means of the verses beginning with "abhāva," that characteristic of perfect awakening is also taught in the Śrīsamāja.
The purification of passion and the other afflictions which was demonstrated in the Paramādya—
that too was taught by the Tathāgatas with reference to universal emptiness.
Whatever reality has been demonstrated in various sūtras and tantras,
it is indeed this state of universal emptiness (sarvaśūnyapada) that is expressed therein, and nothing else.
Within the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma of the Great Sage, that which is the most essential of essences has been proclaimed: the characteristic of perfect enlightenment.
Whether wearing matted hair, naked, or shaven-headed, or possessing a topknot, those who desire full awakening adopt various modes of conduct free from attachment and assume diverse outward signs.
For those who are devoid of reality, the sequence beginning with the practice of vows and so forth—
because it lacks the knowledge of reality— liberation is not attained thereby.
Through the yoga of a beginner, one shall attain the eighth stage;
beholding the three lights, one is established upon the ten stages.
Having attained perfect awakening and reached the Pure Abodes,
one becomes non-retrogressive in the Buddha-fields and attains omniscience in this very life.
The realization of the source of phenomena (dharmodayā) occurs through the expansion of play, passion, and so forth;
the realization of the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu) occurs through activities as they arise.
Through the practice of supreme perfect enlightenment,
yogins here train by means of conduct characterized by the forms of conceptual proliferation and so forth.
"Āḥ! What is the use of the practice of cultivation? Primordial purity is innate;
for it is established by its very nature as suchness, not born of conceptual construction. (Pk 2.83)
Those who, having cast aside the sequence of gnosis here, conceptualize in this way while remaining ignorant of its distinctions, become practitioners once again.
Those who know the distinctions between the manifestations of primordial nature (prakṛti) and rely upon the fourth principle,
yet do not practice in these three ways, shall not quickly attain the fruit.
Just as fire contained within wood does not emerge without friction,
so too enlightenment is not born in this life without practice.
He who is deceitful in mind, indolent, and a reviler of his gurus; whose mind is puffed up with pride because he has received initiation;
whose heart is diminished by the thought that omniscience is not easily attained—that wretched man perceives only the faults of the guru and not his virtues.
Devoid of service, he should not desire the light of reality; rather, with anger, he should move the words of praise.
Upon seeing his teacher in assemblies, he should turn his back; however, when the teacher is in private, he should perform prostrations before him.

And thus, a wise person should never keep near them a wicked disciple who has fallen into such baseness—even one's own biological son—if he is censured by the noble ones; likewise, a Vaiśya or a king [who is so disposed], for they obstruct supreme enlightenment.
Endowed with auspicious qualities, possessing wisdom and diligence, he regards his teachers with devotion as equal to a Buddha;
having realized the Dharma of the Victorious One and being serene toward the teachings, such a person here becomes a worthy vessel—one should bestow favor upon him.

Though he has heard many tantras and is proficient in the Āgamas, having failed to obtain instruction through service to his gurus, that scholar of the scriptures is not capable of accomplishing even his own welfare; thus, that very scripture becomes merely a cause of exhaustion.
Now, there may be one who is fortunate and has received the instruction on reality, yet whose dull intellect is incapable of synthesizing the meaning;
though his mind is intent on the welfare of others and he is engaged in teaching, being devoid of the excellence of speech, he too incurs contempt.

One who has studied many tantras, possesses wisdom, knows the six steps, and is endowed with mindfulness, intelligence, fortitude, intellect, and vigor; having received the instruction on reality through service to the venerable guru—he indeed is capable of explaining the teaching of the King of Tantras.

Through the merit accumulated by Śākyamitra, who has analyzed the path to enlightenment with words clearly composed by the grace of Āryavajra—one who has heard many extensive tantras—may all beings become partakers of awakening through its manifest and potent ripening. Thus, Pk_2.94.
Also known by the alternative name *Anuttarasandhi*,
the *Sarvaśuddhiviśuddhikrama* is completed.
This is the work of the venerable Śākyamitra;
its extent is one hundred [verses].
This is the second sequence. [3]
The third chapter is the Process of Self-Consecration.
Homage to the venerable Vajra Master!
Having prostrated to the supreme Vajra, the leader of Vajrasattva and the others, [I shall explain it].
And the stage of self-consecration shall also be explained by me out of compassion.

First of all, having received empowerment according to the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), knowing the intent of the fourfold tantra, having attained the isolation of body, speech, and mind, possessing a retentive memory, and having conviction in the two truths;
one should properly propitiate the Vajra Guru.
Then, having performed a great feast offering (*gaṇapūjā*) for the pleased Guru and having offered a sixteen-year-old consort (*mudrā*) to the Great Vajra Guru, [one should proceed].

Immediately thereafter, having received the instruction on the sequence of self-consecration from the mouth of the Guru, and then having obtained the secret empowerment along with the bestowing of the garland, water, awakened vajra-bell, mirror, and the permission of the Preceptor (Ācāryānujñā), one should praise the Teacher, the Guru, with these [verses]:
"In your body there is no porosity; there is neither flesh, bone, nor blood."
You have displayed a body in the sky like a rainbow.
In your body there is no impurity, nor does hunger or thirst arise;
yet, for the sake of conforming to the world, you have displayed worldly activities.
Ungraspable like the moon in water, not dependent on any phenomena,
without ego-conceit, free from delusion, and without support— homage be to you!
You are always in a state of meditative equipoise, whether walking, standing, or sleeping;
O supportless one, who remains unattached amidst all paths of envy, homage be to you!
You manifest through great supernatural power by means of the illusion-like samādhi;
having attained the state beyond diversity, O supportless one, homage be to you!
Having thus praised the Vajraguru with his truly existing qualities, one should request him for the sake of hearing [the teaching] with this verse:
"O Omniscient One, mass of primordial wisdom, purifier of the wheel of existence!
O Lord, today, by means of the jewel of your exposition, grant me grace. (Pk 3.7)
O Lord, apart from your lotus feet, there is no other refuge;
therefore, be gracious, O foremost of Buddhas, hero of the world, great sage!
Having heard those words, which were skillful in making a request,
he then gave rise to compassion for his disciples and began the self-consecration.
The stage known as self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna) is the vision of conventional truth;
it is obtained through the grace of the guru’s feet, and not otherwise.
For that practitioner by whom the sequence of self-consecration is not attained,
his exertion in the sūtras, tantras, and ritual manuals is in vain.
Having attained the stage of self-consecration, the Lord, who consists of all Buddhas,
undoubtedly attains Buddhahood in this very life.
The samādhi of self-consecration and likewise the state of luminosity are known as the two truths, distinguished by way of cause and fruit.
For the Clear Light is indeed attained through the sequence of self-consecration;
therefore, the Vajra Master should first demonstrate self-consecration. (Pk 3.14)
The entire world is not independent; indeed, nothing arises independently.
Its cause is luminosity, which is the luminosity of universal emptiness.
By that very mind through which fools have fallen into bondage in saṃsāra,
by that same mind yogins have gone to the state of the Sugatas.
Nothing whatsoever is born here, nor does anyone die;
one should understand that cyclic existence itself abides as the forms and appearances of the mind.
Without the application of the vital wind (*vāyu*), the true nature of the mind (*citta*) is never perceived;
from the mind, due to its being the cause of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), arises the emergence of karma and birth. (3.18)
Furthermore, that same triad of consciousness, when conjoined with the vital wind, arises as the form of yogis; that is called the illusory body (māyā-deha).
Therefore, this entire world is said here to be like an illusion;
established in the illusion-like samādhi, one perceives everything as such.
Form and feeling, perception and mental formations,
and consciousness as the fifth, as well as the four elements.
The sense faculties, the objects, and the fivefold cognition—
all this, whether internal or external, is distinctively nothing but illusion and not otherwise.
One should perceive the illusory body by means of a reflection in a mirror;
the pervasiveness [of the syllables] by means of a rainbow, and [their presence everywhere] by means of the moon in water. (Pk 3.23)
Like a reflection clearly seen in a stainless mirror,
Vajrasattva— liberated from both existence and non-existence— is beautifully depicted.
Endowed with the excellence of all aspects, his form is never-tiring to behold;
he should reveal this to a good disciple—this is called self-consecration.
For this very illusion, characterized by the absence of defects, is what is to be perceived;
it is illusion itself that is the truth of the conventional, and that is the Enjoyment Body (sāmbhogika-kāya).
He alone is the Gandharva-being, for he alone is indeed the Vajra-body;
since he himself is Vajrasattva, one should therefore perform worship to oneself.
The self is indeed all-buddhahood and all-heroism;
therefore, with every effort, one should always worship the self.
One should always regard the application of mantras and mudrās, the conceptualization of mandalas and so forth, and all rituals of offerings and fire-sacrifices as being like an illusion.
One should perform all rites— whether for pacification (śāntika), enrichment (pauṣṭika), subjugation (vaśya), or malevolent magic (abhicārika),
as well as summoning (ākarṣaṇa) and so forth— likewise like a rainbow.
One should engage in the enjoyment of the erotic and other sentiments, the practice of song and instrumental music,
and activity in the arts, like the moon reflected in water.
One should observe the activity of the eye and the other senses toward form, sound, smell, taste, and even the tangible as being like an illusion.
What need is there for much speaking here? For in the Vajrayāna, according to reality, whatever the yogin takes as an object, he should conceive that very thing as being like an illusion.
He who perceives a reflection in a mirror, a dream, an illusion, a bubble,
and a magical trick as being similar [to the world], is known as a Lord (prabhu).
"Just as the world is always seen and touched like an illusion, yet its perception is proclaimed to be merely conventional, like an illusion. (Pk 3.35)
Whatever is the object-path of the senses, that very thing is by its own nature illusion;
through the yoga of non-meditative equipoise, one should carry forth everything as consisting of the Buddha.
Everywhere, from every side, everything, in every way, at all times, and spontaneously,
he beholds his own self as accomplished and consisting of all Buddhas.
Whether walking or standing, the Great Being, the Lord who consists of all bliss,
obtains dwellings, food, drink, and so forth from space in an instant.
They shall become teachers who cut through cyclic existence among the most excellent of people;
they are worshipped by all, including the gods, who prostrate before them again and again.
Just as one is devoted to the Teacher who seeks the welfare of the world's journey,
even so is the great yogin, because he gathers all knowledge and its objects.
Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by one characterized as Vajrasattva;
all the mudrās of great bliss are spontaneously realized.
The afflictions, the paths of action, the body, the agents, and indeed the fruits,
are like a mirage or a dream, and resemble a city of the Gandharvas.
Not knowing this samādhi, they perceive the conventional as truly existent; various diseases arise for them, and illusion is their physician’s remedy.
But he who does not obtain from a guru the instruction on self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna),
having resorted to eternalism or nihilism, shall fall back again.
Having set aside all other forms of worship, one should commence with the worship of the Guru;
for when he is satisfied, that supreme knowledge of the Omniscient One is obtained.
What merit has not been performed by him, or what austerity has not been practiced,
through the worship of the Teacher Vajrasattva, the achiever of the unsurpassed?
Whatever is most beloved and whatever is most excellent, that indeed should be given to the guru by one who desires that very thing to be inexhaustible. (3.47)
The teacher removes evil; the teacher removes fear;
the teacher carries one across to the further shore from the great terror of the ocean of suffering.
One who is smeared with the impurity of egoism, who violates the sequence of reality,
and who is contemptuous toward the dharmas of reality— to such a person, one should not reveal the truth.
One who is truthful in speech, devoted to the guru, solitary, focused on a single goal,
and a protector of the rules of conduct— such a person one should show the Krama.
The third stage, the sequence of self-consecration, is completed.
This is the work of the venerable teacher Nāgārjuna.
Its length is fifty-six [verses].
This is the fourth chapter: The Sequence of Complete Enlightenment.
Homage to Śrī Vajrasattva!
Having paid homage to Vajrasattva, the teacher of universal emptiness,
I shall now explain this fourth stage, the process of manifest enlightenment.
That Blessed One, the Self-Existent, is the sole presiding deity;
however, because he provides the instruction, the Vajrācārya is superior to him.
Having performed that propitiation for a year or even for a month,
one should offer worship according to one's ability to that Guru who has been pleased.
Having offered a well-trained consort to him according to her own nature,
one should perform the worship within the circle of the assembly (gaṇamaṇḍala) according to the ritual procedure.
Then, the great yogi, satisfied by the enjoyment of the five objects of desire,
should bring about the arising of light through the practice of meditative absorption.
Having carefully established the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) within the vase and other vessels,
the Guru should, out of compassion, confer the empowerment upon the excellent disciple at midnight.
Having received the empowerment at the break of dawn,
the disciple, with palms joined in reverence, should worship and propitiate the guru with hymns of praise.
Liberated from the three realms, you have attained equality with space;
you do not descend into desires, O supportless one—homage be to you!
You are not dependent upon the aggregates, the elements, or the sense-bases;
liberated from all inversions and without support, homage be to you!
O you whose intentions are free from conceptualization, whose mind is non-abiding,
whose mental attention is inconceivable, and who are without support— homage be to you!
Without abode like space, free from conceptual proliferation and stainless;
you possess a mind equal to space, O supportless one—homage be to you!
Desiring to behold the perfect awakening whose intrinsic nature is universal emptiness,
the disciple, having offered praise with palms joined, should again exhort the guru.
O Great Lord, grant me the vision of perfect awakening,
which is liberated from karma and birth, and devoid of the three appearances.
Grant me, O Great Teacher, the unsurpassed Vajra-knowledge, the great knowledge of all Buddhas, the abode of all Tathāgatas. (Pk 4.14)
O Great Vajra, grant me that which purifies body, speech, and mind—
beginningless and endless, peaceful, and the purifier of all afflictions.
Thus propitiated by the recitation of his truly existing qualities, the yogin,
having generated compassion for the disciple, should then begin the procedure in this sequence.
The light of night is that which possesses the clear rays of the sun; the light of day is the radiance of sunlight;
and the light of twilight is perceived through its own inherent natures repeatedly.
That which is by nature liberated is neither night, nor twilight, nor is it day.
This is that moment of awakening described by the supreme Guru, accessible only to yogins.

The darkness of night has perished and the entire twilight glow has vanished; for as long as the sun does not rise here, may the preeminent teacher, having destroyed the darkness through his vision of external awakening, reveal the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) to his disciple during this clear moment.
One attains inner bliss, free from all defilement, and the awakening of a Buddha in an instant.
Whether it be beginningless or having a beginning, whether it be without a middle or having a middle,
whether it be endless or having an end— the wise declare all that to be empty.
Where there is neither going nor coming, neither decrease nor increase, nor even non-existence and existence;
it is a state of extreme wonder, a wonder beyond form, which is neither stationary nor transitory.

That which is free from the conventional designations of existence and non-existence, which is neither of the nature of merit nor of the nature of sin, and which is the supreme state consisting of neither merit nor sin— the Buddhas proclaim that to be the universal emptiness.

Having attained such a reality, the yogi—who is the self of all that moves and is stationary, the sole kinsman of the world, and who wanders as the embodiment of wisdom—becomes Nṛsiṃha; he attains an imperishable body throughout the entire universe.
Though his body is crooked, he is not crooked in body; though he has no seat, he is steadfast in the binding of the posture;
though his eyes are closed, they are wide awake; though he is composed, he is not merely composed.

He may be possessed of speech, yet even if not endowed with eloquence; he may be possessed of enjoyments, yet his conduct may be unconventional; he may be a lord of the world, yet he has become the servant of others—he who knows reality and whose every fault is exhausted.
The disciple who has received the instruction should then practice yoga in two ways:
by means of the process of grasping the mass (piṇḍagrāha) and likewise by means of successive penetration (anubheda).
From the head down to the feet, as long as it has reached the heart, the yogin enters the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); this is known as the grasping of the mass (piṇḍagrāha).
Having first rendered both the stationary and the moving worlds luminous, one should subsequently do the same for oneself; for this is the sequence of non-differentiation.
Just as the wind of the breath dissolves from all sides into a mirror,
so too does the yogin repeatedly enter the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, eating, opening or closing his eyes, or laughing, the knower of reality always remains in this yoga of meditation. (Pk 4.29)
The welfare of sentient beings may also sometimes be accomplished by means of rays corresponding to various [forms],
joined with wind and consciousness, through the process of self-consecration.
Just as a fish quickly emerges from clear river water,
so too is the net of illusion projected from the all-empty, which is likewise clear.
The conceptualization of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) and so forth depends upon the five Buddha families;
it arises from the five rays of light like a rainbow in the sky.
Whether one should perform the binding of mudrās or recite mantras,
or even do anything else at all, one should remain established in the state of universal emptiness.
The consumer of all, the seer of all, the one who bows to all,
the all-pervading, the creator of all, and the possessor of all signs— he succeeds through the emptiness of all.
Having received the instruction, the fortunate and excellent disciple— whose mind is indeed called the ultimate reality according to the Baudha tradition—
should receive it once again from the presence of the Guru with palms joined and hands holding flowers.

"One's own mind is free from all entities, devoid of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, as well as the grasped and the grasper; through the equality of the selflessness of phenomena, it is primordially unarisen and has emptiness as its intrinsic nature.
Then, one should give a suitable fee to the guru:
a jewel, a house, an elephant or horse, a village, or a bed and seat.
If one would give away a male servant, a female servant, a beloved wife, a daughter of exquisite beauty,
and even one's own self— what else remains?

Having obtained the grace of the teacher, the yogi of reality—possessing stainless and firm intelligence and realizing the intrinsic nature of all phenomena—should meditate upon the realm of the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa: which is transparent, pure, and exceedingly subtle; composed of supreme Śiva;
free from duality and conceptual construction; and consisting of eternal bliss.
Liberated from merit and demerit, the Blessed One himself is born here as Vajrasattva.
The fourth chapter, the sequence of the realization of the supreme secret bliss, is completed.
This is the work of the venerable master Nāgārjuna.
The extent of this treatise is forty verses.
The fifth [chapter], the Stage of the Union (*yuganaddha*).
Homage to the glorious Vajradhara!
Having prostrated before the Lord who consists of both cause and fruit, and who is free from all duality,
I shall correctly write down the supreme sequence of the Union (yuganaddha).
By abandoning the two conceptual constructions of "saṃsāra" and "nirvāṇa," that state in which they become one is called "yuganaddha" (the yoked pair).
Having understood both affliction and purification from the perspective of ultimate reality,
he who knows their state of oneness knows the union.
If a yogi should practice by unifying the conceptualization of entities with forms and the conceptualization of formlessness, he knows the state of union (*yuganaddha*).
The intellect does not exist as a duality of the grasped and the grasper;
where there is non-differentiation, that is called "yoked-in-pair" (yuganaddha).
But he who proceeds having abandoned the notions of permanence and annihilation truly knows the reality called the "yoked-together" sequence; he is a wise man.
Having realized the unity of wisdom and compassion, wherever one proceeds, this sequence known as "yoked together" (yuganaddha) is the domain of the Buddhas.
Having understood everything in brief through the meditative union of wisdom and means,
that state in which the great yogi abides is the state of "union" (yuganaddha).

Where there is neither that which has a remainder of substrate nor that which is without a remainder of substrate—in this way, no conceptual construction exists; that indeed is the "yoked pair" (yuganaddha).
Wherein there is the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena,
as well as the state of being secluded from conceptual construction— this is the characteristic of the unified pair (yuganaddha).

Having gradually realized the self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) as luminous, the knower of reality [realizes] the union (*samāja*) of those very two; for this is indeed the sequence of the "yoked-together" (*yuganaddha*).
Entry into the abode of suchness occurs through the dissolution of the grasping at a solid mass;
from that arises the state of union (yuganaddha) which pervades everywhere.
Having understood conventionality and ultimate reality separately through their distinctions,
that in which their union occurs is called "yoked together" (yuganaddha).
Likewise, where there is no emergence whatsoever that does not have that very [reality] as its object, that is the state of the yogis, the union (yuganaddha), which is imperishable. (5.14)
Free from these two states of being asleep and awakened,
the Teacher calls that which is devoid of sleep and waking "yuganaddha" (the unified pair).
For the yogi who stands in the union (yuganaddha), there is in every way no such thing as concentration or non-concentration; he is free from both existence and non-existence.
Freed from both non-recollection and recollection, characterized by constant arising,
the yogi, established in the stage of the unified couple (*yuganaddha*), may move about according to his will.
Freed from both passion and dispassion, embodied in supreme bliss,
he who contemplates the union of the two shall remain steadfast as long as saṃsāra endures.
Having made both effect and cause non-different by their very nature,
that state of the yogins which the Buddhas describe is called "the union" (yuganaddha).
This is the generation stage and this is the completion stage;
where there is oneness of these two, that is called "yoked together" (yuganaddha).
Wherever there is no conceptualization that "this deity is pure" or "this [deity] would be impure," that is the state of union (yuganaddha).
By abandoning the two conceptualizations of "having form" and "being formless," the lord of yogis who knows peace has attained the state of union (yuganaddha).
Thus, the yogi who stands established in this way, remaining in the stage of the union of the two,
is indeed called the omniscient one, the seer of reality, and the sustainer of the universe.
Fully awakened through the net of illusion, he has reached the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra;
having accomplished what was to be done, the great yogi abides in the method of the two truths.
This very non-dual gnosis is non-abiding nirvāṇa;
it is likewise Buddhahood, the state of Vajrasattva, and all-pervading sovereignty.
Furthermore, the diamond-like samādhi is indeed the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*).
The diamond-like samādhi is also said to be non-dual.
Terms such as "non-arising" and so forth indicate non-dual gnosis;
they are all designations for this very [gnosis], and nothing else is expressed therein.
By means of this very [path], the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have attained the siddhi whose nature is Mahāmudrā, which is free from the positions of existence and non-existence.
The great yogi, striving and established in the state of union,
should meditate upon union itself and also upon the conduct that follows from it.
As it is with oneself, so it is with the enemy; as it is with one's wife, so it is with one's own son;
as it is with one's mother, so it is with a Vaiśya woman; and as it is with a Ḍombī, so it is with a twice-born woman.
As is clothing, so is skin; as is a jewel, so is chaff;
as is urine, so is liquor; as is cooked rice, so is excrement. (Pk 5.31)
Just as fragrant camphor is like a smell born of impurity,
so a word that offers praise is like a loathsome word.
As is Rudra, so is the Vajrin; as is night, so is day;
as is a dream, so is what is seen; as is what has perished, so is that which remains. (Pk 5.33)
As is happiness, so is suffering; as is a wicked person, so is a son;
as is the Avīci hell, so is heaven; and as is merit, so is sin.
Knowing this, the wise one should act without hesitation, performing all deeds;
by adopting a secret vow, all perfections are accomplished.
"Whatever merit has been obtained by elucidating this unsurpassed Five Stages—by this, may the world sport in the samādhi of the unified pair. (Pk 5.36)
The fifth chapter, on the stage of union, is completed.
This is the work of the venerable master Nāgārjuna.
The extent of this treatise is thirty-five verses.
The *Pañcakrama* is completed.
Having realized the unity of wisdom and compassion, wherever one proceeds, this sequence known as "yoked together" (yuganaddha) is the domain of the Buddhas.
(From the *Pañcakrama*, verses 5–7:
It is like a mass of snow situated within a collection of deep waves stirred by Mount Mandara, which, with its exceedingly intense speed and stable form, revolves with a dense roar.

May Lokeśvara protect you— he who is encircled by the splendor of a dense mass of his own light, and who dwells on the glorious Mount Potalaka, which resounds with the echoes of the proclamation of the profound teachings.
In the *Subhāṣitaratnakośa*, Vidyākara says:
The Middle Way wisdom is neither real nor unreal, nor both, nor neither; it is beyond description and consists of the excellence of all forms.
Victorious is that Goddess, the Conqueror and Teacher, who is the very reality of the stable and moving world; she is self-awareness itself, the beloved of the bliss-vajra.
(In the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, a commentary on the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, by Raviśrī):
"Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa."
May there be auspiciousness.
